title: College
description: Students, courses and the scores they have earned. Some scores are not in yet (NULL).
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, year_of_study INTEGER NOT NULL, branch TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, title TEXT NOT NULL, credits INTEGER NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(id), score INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));
seed: INSERT INTO courses VALUES (1,'CS101','Intro to Programming',4),(2,'CS201','Data Structures',4),(3,'EC101','Circuits',3),(4,'MA101','Calculus',3),(5,'CS301','Databases',3);

problems.title: Scores still pending
problems.statement: Which students have at least one enrollment with **no score yet**? Return each student's `name` once.
problems.expected: SELECT DISTINCT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.score IS NULL
problems.hint: NULL is tested with IS NULL, never with = NULL.
problems.note: Comparisons with NULL are never true, so `score = NULL` returns nothing.

problems.title: Average score per student
problems.statement: Return each student's `name` and the average of their scores rounded to one decimal place (`avg_score`). Students with no scores at all are left out.
problems.expected: SELECT s.name, ROUND(AVG(e.score), 1) AS avg_score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id GROUP BY s.id, s.name HAVING COUNT(e.score) > 0
problems.hint: AVG skips NULL scores. COUNT(score) counts only the non-NULL ones.
problems.note: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. That difference decides many NULL questions.

problems.title: Courses nobody takes
problems.statement: Return the `code` and `title` of courses with **no enrollments**.
problems.expected: SELECT c.code, c.title FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL
problems.hint: LEFT JOIN from courses and keep the unmatched rows.
problems.note: Test a column from the right table that can never be NULL when matched (here the key).

problems.title: Credit load
problems.statement: A student's credit load is the sum of the credits of the courses they are enrolled in. Return `name` and `credits` for students with a load of **10 or more**.
problems.expected: SELECT s.name, SUM(c.credits) AS credits FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id GROUP BY s.id, s.name HAVING SUM(c.credits) >= 10
problems.hint: Join through enrollments to courses, SUM the credits, filter with HAVING.
problems.note: Enrollment rows without a score still count towards the load.

problems.title: Top scorer per course
problems.statement: For each course that has scores, return the course `code`, the `student` with the highest score and that `score`.
problems.expected: SELECT code, student, score FROM (SELECT c.code AS code, s.name AS student, e.score AS score, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.id ORDER BY e.score DESC) AS r FROM enrollments e JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id WHERE e.score IS NOT NULL) WHERE r = 1
problems.hint: Rank scores within each course, ignore NULL scores, keep rank 1.
problems.note: Without the IS NOT NULL filter, NULL scores sort first in some databases and last in others.

problems.title: Pass rate per course
problems.statement: A score of **60 or more passes**. For each course with scores, return its `code` and `pass_rate`: the percentage of scored enrollments that passed, rounded to a whole number. Order by code.
problems.expected: SELECT c.code, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(e.score >= 60) / COUNT(e.score)) AS pass_rate FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id WHERE e.score IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.id, c.code ORDER BY c.code
problems.hint: In SQLite a comparison is 1 or 0, so SUM(score >= 60) counts passes. Divide by the number of scored rows.

problems.title: Second highest score
problems.statement: Return the **second highest distinct score** as a single value called `score`.
problems.expected: SELECT MAX(score) AS score FROM enrollments WHERE score < (SELECT MAX(score) FROM enrollments)
problems.hint: The largest score that is smaller than the largest score.
problems.note: A classic interview question. LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 over DISTINCT scores works too.
